title: How Hard Is Hard Enough? A Better Way to Think About the Last Rep
subtitle: Repetitions in reserve can help you judge effort without turning every set into a test of how much discomfort you can tolerate.
imageAlt: A woman and a man training in a bright community gym, each focused on a controlled dumbbell set while the other waits nearby.
imageConcept: A candid scene in a welcoming, light-filled gym: two friends of different ages and body types train independently at nearby benches, one completing a controlled dumbbell row while the other rests and watches their own form in a mirror. The emphasis is on attentive effort, not strain or competition.
body: The question behind the final rep

A set ends, and the familiar question arrives: Could you have done one more? Two more? None? That judgment matters because training needs enough effort to challenge the body, but “hard” does not have to mean forcing every set until another repetition is impossible. A useful way to describe the distance from that point is repetitions in reserve, or RIR. If you finish a set believing you could have completed two more repetitions with sound technique, you would call it roughly 2 RIR.

RIR is an estimate, not a hidden performance score. It gives you a shared language for effort and a way to adjust a workout to the day you are having. The central point is less dramatic than much gym advice suggests: the last possible rep is not the only rep that counts. Research supports challenging resistance training, but it has not identified one exact stopping point that is best for every person, exercise, or goal.
What counts as a rep in reserve?

Imagine doing a set of eight squats. At the end, ask how many additional repetitions you could perform while keeping the same basic movement quality—not how many you could grind out by changing your depth, losing balance, or turning the exercise into something else. If the honest estimate is two clean reps, that is about 2 RIR. If you feel certain you could continue for several more, the set was farther from your limit.

That “clean rep” condition matters. Failure is described in different ways across research and training settings, and people do not always mean the same thing when they say a set was taken to failure. For practical purposes, judge the set against the technique and range of motion you intended to use. RIR scales have been used as a feasible way to prescribe and adjust training intensity, but the evidence also highlights accuracy as a consideration [3]. Think of the number as a useful estimate, not a precise measurement.
What the evidence says—and does not say

The 2026 American College of Sports Medicine position stand synthesized 137 systematic reviews involving more than 30,000 participants. Its broad finding is reassuring: lifting to momentary fatigue was not consistently better and was not necessary for the outcomes reviewed. The stand describes near-failure work, including around 2–3 RIR, as ways to achieve sufficient effort, while cautioning that evidence does not establish one exact RIR target for everyone [1].

A 2024 dose–response analysis found strength gains were similar across a wide range of estimated proximity to failure. Muscle-growth outcomes showed a different pattern: hypertrophy tended to increase as sets ended closer to failure, though the authors describe the analysis as exploratory and say the exact relationship remains unclear [2]. Taken together, these findings do not produce a universal rule. They suggest that chasing the final rep may be less important for strength than consistent, appropriately challenging training, while getting closer to failure may matter more when muscle growth is a priority. Even then, “closer” is not the same as “every set must end at failure.”
Why your goal and exercise change the answer

If your priority is getting stronger, you need practice producing force and a training plan you can repeat. A set that leaves a little room can still be demanding, and stopping before technique deteriorates may help preserve good-quality work across the session. If your priority is muscle growth, working nearer to your limit may be useful, but that does not make maximal effort compulsory on every exercise or every set.

Exercise choice also changes the practical risk. A final hard repetition on a stable machine may be easier to manage than one on a heavy squat or bench press without appropriate safety arrangements. Your training history, equipment, sleep, stress, and how you feel that day can all shape what a given effort feels like. That is why RIR is better treated as a dial than a fixed setting: it helps you communicate and adjust, rather than ordering you to stop at precisely the same number every time.
A practical way to use RIR

For your next few sessions, try this simple process. First, choose a load you can lift with controlled technique for the planned repetition range. During the set, focus on the movement rather than trying to calculate RIR after every repetition. At the end, ask: “How many more repetitions like those could I have done?” Record your best estimate next to the exercise and load.

Start by observing rather than forcing a target. If you repeatedly finish a set feeling you could have done many more clean reps, you might add a small amount of weight next time or continue for a few more reps, provided that fits your plan. If the final repetitions become unstable or painful, stop; do not count a compromised rep as proof that you reached the right effort. For a safer calibration, use a stable machine or a light-to-moderate load and occasionally compare your estimate with a few additional controlled repetitions. You do not need to test this on heavy free-weight lifts, and you do not need to turn a normal workout into a failure test.

RIR becomes more informative when you look for patterns over time. If a set you call 3 RIR consistently leaves you able to do five more repetitions, your estimate may be conservative. If you often expect two more but cannot complete even one without losing form, you may be underestimating how close you are. That is normal; people are not equally accurate on every exercise or at every load. A review of RIR research found the method workable, while also identifying assessment and accuracy as issues to consider [3].

Make a brief note of the exercise, load, completed reps, and estimated RIR. After several sessions, use those records to make small adjustments rather than reacting to one unusually good or difficult day. If fatigue is accumulating or your form is slipping, reduce the load, stop the set earlier, or take more rest. If you are recovering well and the work feels too easy, gradually increase the challenge. The goal is not to become perfect at predicting your limit. It is to make training decisions a little more deliberate.
A better question than “Did I go all out?”

After a set, try asking: “Was that challenging enough for the goal, and could I repeat this quality of work?” That question leaves room for effort without glorifying exhaustion. For strength, the answer may be a demanding set that ends before a grind. For muscle growth, you may choose to work closer to your limit on some sets, while keeping technique and safe setup in view. On a day when energy is low, a sound set with more reps in reserve can be a sensible adjustment—not a failed workout.

RIR offers structure without pretending the body is a spreadsheet. Start with an honest estimate, pay attention to the movement you can control, and let your training log teach you how your own effort feels. The last possible repetition can have a place in training, but it does not need to be the price of admission.
